stem: A 72-year-old woman tripped at home and landed on her outstretched left arm. An X-ray in the emergency department shows a fracture through the surgical neck of the humerus. Pinprick sensation is reduced over a small patch on the outer aspect of the upper arm just below the point of the shoulder. Sensation in the forearm and hand is normal, and she can extend her wrist and fingers. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
why_correct: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, so it is vulnerable in fractures here and in anterior shoulder dislocation. It supplies deltoid and teres minor and gives sensation to the regimental badge area over the lateral upper arm. Reduced sensation in exactly this patch after a surgical neck fracture points to axillary nerve injury.
why_wrong: A. Radial nerve injury follows mid-shaft fractures and causes wrist drop, but her wrist extension is intact. B. The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus and has no cutaneous area on the lateral arm. C. Long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula without arm numbness. D. Musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion and numbs the lateral forearm, not the shoulder.
pearl: Always test and document regimental badge sensation in surgical neck fractures and shoulder dislocations, both before and after any manipulation.
thinking: Fall onto outstretched arm ↓ Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus ↓ Nerve that wraps around the surgical neck ↓ Numb patch over lateral upper arm: regimental badge area ↓ Axillary nerve
exam_trap: A, radial nerve — the best-known nerve injury with humeral fractures, but it follows mid-shaft fractures and causes wrist drop; her wrist extension is normal.
takeaway: Surgical neck fracture with a numb regimental badge area: axillary nerve injury.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 9 Oct 2026 (held pack H01). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with normal CT
stem: A 38-year-old man was lifting weights at the gym when he felt a sudden, severe pain at the back of his head, reaching its worst within a few seconds. He vomited and went home to rest, coming to the emergency department the following morning. A non-contrast CT head performed 14 hours after the onset of the headache is normal. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Discharge with analgesia and GP follow-up
options.C: Lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia
options.E: Start IV antibiotics for possible meningitis

correct_answer: C. Lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia
why_correct: A thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds must be investigated for subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT is less sensitive when it is performed more than 6 hours after onset, so a normal scan does not exclude bleeding. NICE advises considering lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset to look for xanthochromia, so it can be done now.
why_wrong: A. Discharge before subarachnoid haemorrhage has been excluded is unsafe. B. MRI is not the standard next test for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage after a normal CT. D. Repeating the CT does not improve sensitivity as blood is cleared and becomes harder to see. E. There is no fever or other feature to suggest meningitis.
pearl: Xanthochromia takes about 12 hours to develop, so lumbar puncture is timed for at least 12 hours after headache onset; earlier samples can be falsely reassuring.
thinking: Sudden severe headache peaking in seconds ↓ Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage ↓ CT done late is normal ↓ Late CT can miss blood ↓ Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia
exam_trap: A, discharge — a normal CT and normal examination feel reassuring, but a late CT can miss subarachnoid haemorrhage and a missed bleed can be fatal.
takeaway: Thunderclap headache with a normal late CT: lumbar puncture for xanthochromia.
review_note: answer hinges on movable time thresholds; needs reframing or confirmation against NICE NG228 (dropped from pack 09, 17 Oct 2026)

stem: A 49-year-old man comes to the emergency department on crutches the morning after a wedding reception. Overnight the joint at the base of his left great toe became so tender that he could not bear to pull a sock over it. The joint is swollen, and the skin over it is shiny and dusky red. He is afebrile and otherwise well, with no history of injury. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden overnight onset of severe pain, swelling and shiny red skin over the first metatarsophalangeal joint, after an evening of likely heavy eating and drinking, is the classic picture of acute gout. The first MTP joint is the commonest site of a first attack. Joint aspiration for crystals confirms it, but the clinical picture here is typical.
why_wrong: B. Septic arthritis must be considered in any hot joint, but it usually affects a systemically unwell patient and the first MTP joint is an uncommon site. C. Cellulitis causes spreading redness of the skin and soft tissue rather than pain centred on the joint itself. D. Hallux valgus causes chronic deformity and pressure pain, not an acute inflammatory attack overnight. E. Calcium pyrophosphate disease mainly affects the knee and wrist of older adults.
pearl: Alcohol, particularly beer, and purine-rich meals can trigger acute gout; colchicine or an NSAID started early shortens the attack.
thinking: Sudden overnight acute monoarthritis ↓ first MTP joint, exquisite tenderness, shiny red skin ↓ heavy food and alcohol intake, afebrile and well ↓ Gout
exam_trap: B, septic arthritis — the joint is hot and exquisitely tender, but he is afebrile and well and the site is classic for gout; aspirate if any doubt remains.
takeaway: Sudden, exquisitely painful swelling of the big toe joint in a well man is acute gout until shown otherwise.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15149). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit having taken an overdose the previous evening. She has vomited repeatedly, is sweaty, and describes a constant buzzing in her ears with muffled hearing. A venous blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap. Which drug did she most likely take?
why_correct: Vomiting, sweating, tinnitus with reduced hearing and a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis after an overdose point to aspirin. Salicylates disrupt cellular metabolism, producing acid, and directly affect the inner ear. A salicylate level guides treatment such as urinary alkalinisation or haemodialysis in severe cases.
why_wrong: A. Amitriptyline causes drowsiness, anticholinergic signs, seizures and arrhythmias rather than tinnitus. B. Paracetamol causes delayed liver injury and does not cause tinnitus. C. Iron causes vomiting and acidosis but not tinnitus or hearing change. D. Lithium toxicity causes tremor, ataxia and confusion rather than tinnitus with acidosis.
pearl: Tinnitus or deafness after an overdose should prompt a salicylate level, even when the patient does not name the drug taken.
thinking: Overdose with repeated vomiting ↓ tinnitus and muffled hearing ↓ raised anion gap metabolic acidosis ↓ combination fits salicylate toxicity ↓ Aspirin
exam_trap: C, Iron sulfate — iron overdose also causes vomiting and a metabolic acidosis, but it does not affect hearing, which is the discriminating clue.
takeaway: Overdose with vomiting, acidosis and ear symptoms suggests aspirin: check a salicylate level.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ14832). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 64-year-old woman attends her GP because she now has to stop for breath halfway up the hill to the shops. She has had a morning cough with small amounts of clear sputum for several winters and needed antibiotics twice last year for chest infections. She smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years and stopped last year. There is no history of childhood wheeze or hay fever. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an obstructive pattern with only a small change after salbutamol. Which condition best accounts for her symptoms?
why_correct: Progressive exertional breathlessness and a chronic productive cough in a long-term smoker, with airflow obstruction that persists after a bronchodilator, is COPD. The minimal bronchodilator response and lack of atopic history point away from asthma. Management includes smoking cessation support, pulmonary rehabilitation where appropriate, vaccinations and inhaled therapy.
why_wrong: A. Asthma usually shows variable symptoms and marked bronchodilator reversibility, often with an atopic history. B. Bronchiectasis causes daily copious purulent sputum and is confirmed on CT, not suggested by small amounts of clear sputum. C. Heart failure causes breathlessness with orthopnoea and oedema, not fixed airflow obstruction on spirometry. E. Pulmonary fibrosis causes a restrictive pattern with fine inspiratory crackles, not obstruction.
pearl: COPD is diagnosed clinically in a person with risk factors and confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry showing airflow obstruction; a large bronchodilator response should make you reconsider asthma.
thinking: Long-term smoker in middle age ↓ chronic morning cough, recurrent winter infections and progressive exertional breathlessness ↓ obstructive spirometry with little bronchodilator response ↓ no atopic or childhood history ↓ COPD
exam_trap: A, Asthma — obstructive spirometry and wheezy chest infections tempt towards asthma, but the persistent obstruction after salbutamol, heavy smoking history and lack of atopy fit COPD.
takeaway: Persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction in a long-term smoker with chronic cough and breathlessness is COPD.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15631). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: An 18-year-old woman visits her practice nurse before moving into university halls of residence. Her records show she was absent from school on the day of the Year 9 meningococcal immunisation and has never had it since. She is otherwise fully immunised. She asks which vaccine will protect her against the meningococcal groups covered by the routine teenage programme. Which vaccine should be offered?
why_correct: The routine UK adolescent programme includes the MenACWY conjugate vaccine, which protects against meningococcal groups A, C, W and Y and reduces carriage in teenagers. Those who missed it remain eligible for a catch-up dose up to their 25th birthday, and first-time university entrants are specifically encouraged to have it. She should be offered MenACWY now.
why_wrong: A. MenB vaccine is given in the infant programme and does not protect against groups A, C, W or Y. B. Hib/MenC covers only group C, and is not the adolescent vaccine. C. HPV vaccine protects against human papillomavirus, not meningococcal disease. E. Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine protects against pneumococcus and is used mainly for older and at-risk groups.
pearl: MenACWY is the routine teenage meningococcal vaccine, and people who missed it can catch up until their 25th birthday. Encourage it before university.
thinking: Teenager who missed the school meningococcal dose ↓ moving into shared university accommodation ↓ adolescent vaccine covers groups A, C, W and Y ↓ catch-up eligibility applies ↓ MenACWY conjugate vaccine
exam_trap: A, MenB vaccine — it tempts because group B is an important cause of meningococcal disease, but MenB is part of the infant schedule and does not cover the groups in the adolescent programme.
takeaway: Missed the teenage meningococcal dose? Offer MenACWY catch-up, especially before university.

stem: A 74-year-old woman develops sudden severe mid-back pain while bending to lift a bag of shopping. She has had no fall or other injury. A spinal X-ray shows a wedge compression fracture of the T12 vertebra. She has no weight loss or night sweats, and her full blood count, calcium, ESR and serum protein electrophoresis are all normal. Which underlying condition is most likely?
why_correct: A vertebral compression fracture from minimal stress, such as bending or lifting, in an older woman is a fragility fracture, and osteoporosis is the most likely cause. Normal blood count, calcium, ESR and protein electrophoresis make malignancy unlikely. She should have a fracture risk assessment with DXA scanning and be considered for bone-protective treatment, calcium and vitamin D.
why_wrong: A. Myeloma can cause vertebral collapse, but normal blood count, calcium, ESR and electrophoresis make it unlikely. B. Osteomalacia causes bone pain, muscle weakness and abnormal calcium, phosphate or vitamin D. C. Metastases are unlikely with no cancer history, no systemic features and normal bloods. D. Paget disease causes bone pain and deformity with a raised alkaline phosphatase, not typical wedge fractures.
pearl: Many vertebral fragility fractures are found incidentally or dismissed as back strain; a vertebral fracture strongly predicts future hip and wrist fractures.
thinking: Older woman with minimal-trauma vertebral fracture ↓ fragility fracture ↓ normal FBC, calcium, ESR, electrophoresis ↓ malignancy unlikely ↓ osteoporosis, arrange DXA and bone protection
exam_trap: A, multiple myeloma — it is a classic cause of vertebral collapse in older people, but the normal blood count, calcium, ESR and electrophoresis argue strongly against it.
takeaway: A low-trauma fracture in an older adult is a fragility fracture; assess for osteoporosis.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15541). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Dry mouth, dry eyes and parotid swelling
stem: A 52-year-old woman tells her GP that her eyes feel gritty all the time, she needs a drink of water to swallow dry food such as crackers, and she keeps a glass by her bed at night. Over the past year she has had several bouts of tender swelling in front of both ears. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Persistent dry eyes and dry mouth with recurrent parotid swelling in a middle-aged woman are characteristic of Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune disease of the exocrine glands. Investigations include anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies and specialist rheumatology assessment. It also carries an increased risk of lymphoma, so persistent gland enlargement needs review.
why_wrong: A. Mumps causes an acute, self-limiting parotitis with fever rather than chronic dryness and recurrent episodes. B. Systemic sclerosis mainly causes skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon and organ fibrosis. C. A salivary stone causes unilateral swelling with meals and does not cause dry eyes. E. Rheumatoid arthritis can be associated with secondary Sjögren syndrome but would present with inflammatory joint disease.
pearl: Dry eyes plus dry mouth with parotid swelling suggests Sjögren syndrome; check anti-Ro and anti-La and remember the increased lymphoma risk.
thinking: Middle-aged woman ↓ Gritty dry eyes and dry mouth ↓ Recurrent bilateral parotid swelling ↓ Autoimmune exocrine gland disease ↓ Sjögren syndrome
exam_trap: C, salivary gland calculus — gland swelling suggests obstruction, but a stone is usually unilateral, meal-related and does not cause dry eyes.
takeaway: Chronic dry eyes and dry mouth with parotid swelling point to Sjögren syndrome.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15920). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 38-year-old woman tells her GP that for the past eight months her periods have been so heavy that she floods through pads, passes clots and has to change protection overnight. Her cycle is regular, and she has no bleeding between periods or after sex. Her cervical screening is up to date and abdominal examination is normal. Which investigation should be offered to her routinely?
why_correct: NICE advises that all women presenting with heavy menstrual bleeding should have a full blood count, because chronic blood loss commonly causes iron-deficiency anaemia that may need treatment in its own right. Further tests are guided by the history and examination rather than done routinely. With a regular cycle, no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and a normal examination, she may be offered treatment without further investigation.
why_wrong: A. Ultrasound is reserved for women with a suspected structural cause, such as an enlarged uterus or pelvic mass on examination. C. Ferritin is not routinely needed; the full blood count is the recommended first test. D. Thyroid tests are indicated only if there are other features of thyroid disease. E. Coagulation testing is for women with features suggesting a bleeding disorder, such as heavy periods since menarche or other bleeding problems.
pearl: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on a woman's quality of life rather than by measured blood loss; a full blood count is the one routine test.
thinking: Heavy, regular periods with clots and flooding ↓ No intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, normal examination ↓ Main routine concern is anaemia from blood loss ↓ Full blood count
exam_trap: C, Serum ferritin — iron deficiency is the worry, so measuring iron stores seems logical, but guidance recommends a full blood count for everyone and does not advise routine ferritin testing.
takeaway: Every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding needs a full blood count; other tests depend on the history.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ14798). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Adrenal insufficiency after stopping long-term steroids
stem: A 58-year-old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica has taken prednisolone for ten months. Feeling much better, she stopped her tablets suddenly last week without telling anyone. She now attends the GP with profound fatigue, nausea, loss of appetite and dizziness when she stands. She has no shoulder or hip girdle stiffness. Her blood pressure is low and falls further on standing. Which is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Adrenal insufficiency from suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis

correct_answer: A. Adrenal insufficiency from suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
why_correct: Prolonged glucocorticoid therapy suppresses ACTH release, and the adrenal glands atrophy and cannot produce enough cortisol when the drug is stopped abruptly. The result is adrenal insufficiency, with fatigue, nausea and hypotension, which can progress to a life-threatening adrenal crisis. Steroids taken for more than a few weeks should be withdrawn gradually, and patients should carry a steroid emergency card and be warned not to stop suddenly.
why_wrong: B. A relapse of polymyalgia would cause recurrent girdle pain and stiffness, which she does not have. C. Steroid-induced hyperglycaemia occurs while taking steroids and improves after stopping them. D. Hypothyroidism develops gradually and is not caused by stopping prednisolone. E. A perforated ulcer causes sudden severe abdominal pain and peritonism.
pearl: Patients on long-term oral steroids should have sick day rules explained and carry a steroid emergency card so that emergency hydrocortisone is not delayed.
thinking: Months of prednisolone ↓ Abrupt self-discontinuation ↓ Fatigue, nausea and postural hypotension without girdle symptoms ↓ Adrenal insufficiency from HPA axis suppression
exam_trap: B, relapse of polymyalgia rheumatica — tempting because symptoms began after stopping treatment, but relapse would bring back girdle pain and stiffness, not nausea and hypotension.
takeaway: Never stop long-term steroids abruptly; HPA suppression can cause adrenal insufficiency and crisis.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15361). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because over several days she has become muddled, nauseated and unsteady on her feet. Indapamide was started for hypertension four weeks ago. She has no urinary symptoms and appears clinically euvolaemic. Blood tests show a markedly low sodium and a low potassium; glucose and calcium are normal. Which is the most likely cause?

options.C: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion from lung cancer

why_correct: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide impair the kidney's ability to dilute urine and commonly cause hyponatraemia, especially in older women and in the first weeks of treatment. Coexisting hypokalaemia supports a diuretic cause. The drug should be stopped and the sodium corrected cautiously to avoid osmotic demyelination.
why_wrong: A. Addison's disease causes hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypotension, not hypokalaemia. B. Infection can cause delirium in older people, but she has no urinary symptoms and this would not explain the electrolyte pattern. C. SIADH from cancer is possible but less likely than a recently started drug known to cause hyponatraemia. D. Hypothyroidism is an uncommon cause of hyponatraemia and would not explain hypokalaemia.
pearl: Always check sodium and potassium within a few weeks of starting a thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic in an older person.
thinking: Older woman with confusion and unsteadiness ↓ Thiazide-like diuretic started recently ↓ Low sodium with low potassium, euvolaemic ↓ Indapamide-induced hyponatraemia
exam_trap: B, urinary tract infection with delirium — tempting because infection is a common cause of confusion in older people, but there are no urinary symptoms and the electrolytes point to the new diuretic.
takeaway: New confusion soon after starting a thiazide-like diuretic: check sodium and suspect drug-induced hyponatraemia.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15208). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 59-year-old woman attends her GP for a blood pressure review. Amlodipine was started two months ago. Since then both ankles become puffy by the evening, improving overnight. She has no breathlessness on exertion or lying flat. Her jugular venous pressure is not raised, her chest is clear, her calves are soft and non-tender, and urine dipstick is negative for protein. Which is the most likely cause of her ankle swelling?
why_correct: Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as amlodipine dilate precapillary arterioles, raising capillary pressure and causing dependent ankle oedema. It is common, dose-related and occurs without signs of fluid overload. Options include reducing the dose or switching or adding another antihypertensive; diuretics are generally ineffective for this type of oedema.
why_wrong: B. Heart failure would usually cause breathlessness, orthopnoea, a raised JVP or crackles. C. Bilateral DVT is uncommon and would cause calf pain and tenderness rather than symmetrical evening swelling. D. Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy proteinuria, which is absent. E. Hypothyroidism causes non-pitting swelling with other systemic features and is not linked to starting amlodipine.
pearl: Ankle oedema from amlodipine responds poorly to diuretics because it is caused by vasodilation, not fluid retention.
thinking: Bilateral ankle swelling after starting amlodipine ↓ No breathlessness, normal JVP and clear chest ↓ No proteinuria or calf tenderness ↓ Calcium-channel blocker-induced peripheral oedema
exam_trap: B, heart failure — tempting because ankle swelling is a classic sign of it, but she has no breathlessness, a normal JVP and a clear chest.
takeaway: Bilateral ankle oedema without fluid overload soon after starting amlodipine is a drug adverse effect.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15209). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 72-year-old man is reviewed on a stroke rehabilitation ward three weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Nursing staff report that he coughs and splutters during meals and his voice sounds wet and gurgly after drinks. He has had two chest infections since admission. Which underlying problem best explains these findings?

options.E: Hospital-acquired infection from poor hand hygiene

correct_answer: A. Aspiration due to unsafe swallowing
why_correct: Coughing while eating and drinking, a wet voice after swallowing and recurrent chest infections indicate dysphagia with aspiration, a common complication after stroke. Oral intake should be reviewed and his swallow formally reassessed by a speech and language therapist, who can advise on safe food and fluid textures and positioning.
why_wrong: B. Reflux causes heartburn and regurgitation, not coughing during swallowing with a wet voice. C. Heart failure causes breathlessness and orthopnoea, not symptoms linked to eating. D. Bronchiectasis causes chronic daily productive cough and would not begin with a stroke. E. Hospital infection does not explain coughing specifically during meals.
pearl: Patients with acute stroke should have their swallow screened before receiving any food, fluid or oral medication, with specialist assessment if the screen is failed.
thinking: Recent stroke ↓ coughing during meals and wet voice after drinks ↓ recurrent chest infections ↓ aspiration from unsafe swallowing
exam_trap: E, hospital-acquired infection from poor hand hygiene — recurrent inpatient chest infections tempt this, but the link to eating and a wet voice points to aspiration.
takeaway: Coughing on eating, a wet voice and recurrent chest infections after stroke mean aspiration: get a swallow assessment.

stem: A 72-year-old man with lung cancer receiving palliative care is visited at home by his GP. Over three days he has become unsteady and both legs feel numb from his navel downwards. He has a mid-back pain that is worse when he coughs. He has not passed urine since the morning and a tender, distended bladder is palpable. He is fully orientated. Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?
why_correct: Back pain worse on coughing with progressive leg symptoms, a sensory level on the trunk and urinary retention in a patient with cancer are features of spinal cord compression. Lung cancer frequently spreads to the spine. Even in palliative care, prompt recognition matters because urgent treatment can preserve mobility and continence and improve quality of life.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia causes confusion, thirst, constipation and fatigue, not a sensory level. C. Brain metastases cause headache, seizures or focal weakness, not a sensory level with retention in an orientated patient. D. Peripheral neuropathy causes glove-and-stocking sensory loss, not a truncal level or retention. E. Opioids can cause retention but do not explain leg numbness with a sensory level.
pearl: A sensory level on the trunk localises the problem to the spinal cord. A level at the umbilicus corresponds to the T10 dermatome, and because cord segments lie higher than their matching vertebrae, the compressing lesion is at or above that level and often at a higher vertebral level than expected.
thinking: Known lung cancer ↓ mid-back pain worse on coughing ↓ leg numbness with a truncal sensory level ↓ urinary retention ↓ metastatic spinal cord compression
exam_trap: E, opioid-induced urinary retention — palliative patients on opioids often retain urine, but this does not explain the sensory level and unsteadiness.
takeaway: A sensory level with leg weakness and retention in cancer means spinal cord compression.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ16053). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: At her booking appointment, a 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is found to be blood group O RhD-negative with no red cell antibodies. Her partner is RhD-positive. The midwife explains that she will be offered routine anti-D immunoglobulin in the third trimester. What is the main purpose of this treatment?

options.B: To prevent maternal sensitisation to fetal RhD antigen
options.C: To prevent ABO incompatibility in the newborn
options.D: To reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia
options.E: To neutralise anti-D antibodies she already has

correct_answer: B. To prevent maternal sensitisation to fetal RhD antigen
why_correct: If an RhD-negative woman is exposed to RhD-positive fetal red cells, she may produce anti-D antibodies that cross the placenta and cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, mainly in later pregnancies. Anti-D immunoglobulin clears fetal red cells from her circulation before her immune system responds. Routine antenatal prophylaxis, together with doses after sensitising events and after birth if the baby is RhD-positive, greatly reduces this risk.
why_wrong: A. Anti-D is preventive and does not treat fetal anaemia, which needs specialist fetal medicine care. C. Anti-D has no effect on ABO incompatibility. D. Anti-D does not affect the risk of pre-eclampsia. E. Anti-D cannot reverse sensitisation once a woman has formed her own antibodies.
pearl: Give anti-D after potentially sensitising events such as abdominal trauma, bleeding after 12 weeks, external cephalic version and amniocentesis, in addition to routine prophylaxis.
thinking: RhD-negative mother, RhD-positive partner ↓ Fetus may be RhD-positive ↓ Fetal cells entering maternal circulation ↓ Anti-D clears them before an immune response ↓ Prevents maternal sensitisation
exam_trap: A, treat existing fetal anaemia — anti-D is associated with haemolytic disease, but it is prophylactic and only works before the mother has been sensitised.
takeaway: Anti-D prevents RhD-negative mothers from becoming sensitised to fetal RhD-positive cells.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15236). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the GP because several children at her nursery have been unwell. She has had a mild fever for two days and very itchy spots that started on her scalp and chest. On examination there are red papules, clear fluid-filled blisters and crusted lesions side by side, mostly on the trunk, with a few shallow ulcers inside her mouth. Her palms and soles are spared. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chickenpox causes intensely itchy crops of lesions that progress from papules to vesicles to crusts, so lesions at different stages are seen together. The rash is concentrated on the trunk, scalp and face and may involve the mouth. Management is usually supportive, with advice on keeping her away from nursery until all lesions have crusted.
why_wrong: A. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes mouth ulcers with vesicles on the hands and feet, which are spared here. B. Measles causes a maculopapular rash that starts behind the ears, with cough, conjunctivitis and coryza. C. Impetigo causes honey-crusted lesions, usually around the nose and mouth, not widespread vesicles. E. Scarlet fever causes a fine sandpaper-like rash with a strawberry tongue and sore throat.
pearl: Lesions at different stages concentrated on the trunk point to chickenpox. Avoid NSAIDs in chickenpox because of the association with severe skin infection.
thinking: Nursery outbreak, mild fever ↓ Very itchy rash starting on scalp and chest ↓ Papules, vesicles and crusts together ↓ Truncal distribution, palms spared ↓ Chickenpox
exam_trap: A, hand, foot and mouth disease — mouth ulcers with vesicles in a nursery child suggest it, but the truncal rash with crops at different stages and spared palms and soles fit chickenpox.
takeaway: Itchy truncal crops of papules, vesicles and crusts together indicate chickenpox.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department with severe central abdominal pain, vomiting, dark urine and weakness of both arms. She also seems anxious and briefly hallucinated overnight. Acute intermittent porphyria is suspected and the ward team is writing her drug chart. Which of the following should be avoided?

options.D: A medicine listed as porphyrinogenic, such as certain anticonvulsants

correct_answer: D. A medicine listed as porphyrinogenic, such as certain anticonvulsants
why_correct: Porphyrinogenic medicines induce hepatic ALA synthase and can worsen or prolong an acute attack, so they must be avoided. Many anticonvulsants, some antibiotics and hormonal preparations fall into this group, and the UK porphyria drug database should be checked before prescribing. Opioids, paracetamol and intravenous glucose are generally regarded as safe.
why_wrong: A. Glucose suppresses ALA synthase and is part of supportive treatment. B. Morphine is considered safe and is commonly needed for the severe pain. C. Paracetamol is considered safe in acute porphyria. E. Sodium chloride is safe and may be needed because hyponatraemia is common in attacks.
pearl: Hyponatraemia from SIADH is common in acute porphyria attacks and can cause seizures; managing these is challenging because many anticonvulsants are themselves porphyrinogenic.
thinking: Abdominal pain, dark urine, motor neuropathy ↓ Psychiatric symptoms ↓ Suspected acute porphyria ↓ Drugs that induce ALA synthase worsen attacks ↓ Avoid porphyrinogenic medicines
exam_trap: B, Morphine for pain — opioids feel risky in someone with neuropsychiatric symptoms, but they are considered safe in porphyria and adequate analgesia is essential.
takeaway: In suspected acute porphyria, check every medicine against a porphyria-safe list and avoid porphyrinogenic drugs.
review_note: key option is near-tautological; needs rewriting as specific drugs and a check against the UK porphyria drug database (dropped from pack 04, 17 Oct 2026)

stem: A 48-year-old woman saw a private gastroenterologist, who recommended a branded version of omeprazole for her reflux. At her GP practice she is told the NHS prescription will be issued generically, and she asks whether the generic will work as well. What is the key principle to explain?

options.A: Branded medicines are safer than generic versions
options.B: The generic contains the same active ingredient as the branded product
options.C: Generic medicines usually work less well than brands
options.D: Generic prescribing needs specialist approval on the NHS
options.E: The generic is a similar but chemically different compound

correct_answer: B. The generic contains the same active ingredient as the branded product
why_correct: A generic medicine contains the same active ingredient as the branded version and is required to be bioequivalent, so it produces the same therapeutic effect. Prescribing by generic name is standard NHS practice and helps reduce cost without reducing effectiveness. She can expect the same benefit from generic omeprazole.
why_wrong: A. Branding does not make a medicine safer; both must meet the same standards. C. Generics are not inherently less effective, as bioequivalence must be shown. D. Generic prescribing is routine and needs no specialist approval. E. The active ingredient is identical, not a different compound.
pearl: Generic prescribing is encouraged across the NHS; brand prescribing is reserved for situations where formulations are not interchangeable.
thinking: Patient worried generic is inferior ↓ Generic contains the same active ingredient ↓ Must be bioequivalent ↓ Same expected therapeutic effect ↓ Generic prescribing is routine NHS practice
exam_trap: A, Branded medicines are safer — many patients assume a brand means higher quality, but generics must meet the same regulatory standards for quality and safety.
takeaway: A generic medicine has the same active ingredient as the brand and is expected to work the same way.

stem: At a community pharmacy, a 63-year-old woman asks to buy naproxen for a flare of lower back pain. On questioning she says she was treated for a bleeding duodenal ulcer two years ago. The pharmacist advises against it and suggests she speaks to her GP. What is the main reason for this advice?
correct_answer: C. Recurrent ulceration with gastrointestinal bleeding
why_correct: NSAIDs block cyclo-oxygenase and reduce the prostaglandins that protect the stomach and duodenal lining. A previous ulcer, especially one that bled, is one of the strongest risk factors for NSAID-related ulceration and bleeding. NICE CKS advises avoiding NSAIDs in people with a history of peptic ulcer, or using gastroprotection and specialist advice if one cannot be avoided.
why_wrong: A. Gum overgrowth is linked to phenytoin, ciclosporin and calcium channel blockers, not NSAIDs. B. NSAIDs do not usually cause hypoglycaemia. D. Hearing loss is a feature of aminoglycosides and loop diuretics, not standard NSAID doses. E. NSAIDs do not affect thyroid function.
pearl: The highest risk of NSAID-related gastrointestinal bleeding is in people over 65, people with previous ulcer or bleeding, and people also taking anticoagulants, antiplatelets, SSRIs or corticosteroids.
thinking: Request for an over-the-counter NSAID ↓ Past bleeding duodenal ulcer ↓ NSAIDs reduce protective mucosal prostaglandins ↓ High risk of recurrent ulcer and bleeding ↓ Advise avoidance and a GP review
exam_trap: D, Sensorineural hearing loss — ototoxicity is a known drug adverse effect so it sounds credible, but it belongs to aminoglycosides and high-dose loop diuretics, not naproxen.
takeaway: A previous peptic ulcer, especially one that bled, is a strong reason to avoid NSAIDs because of the risk of further ulceration and bleeding.
